rationale: A wins because it gives the founder more usable newsroom strategy, not just cleaner summaries: "The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code" is a risky headline, but it opens a real enterprise procurement and security lane and then names the proof that would make or kill it. B has solid work, especially "Figma puts a price on AI: a new $25-a-month seat on top of existing plans," but its lead angle leans on "first big swing" and "bet on staying independent," both bigger than the supplied facts. A has its own overreach, but it exposes the hard proof gates instead of hiding behind tidy three-angle safety.
gaps_in_A: "first substantive product move framed against the collapsed Adobe acquisition" is not in the fact block. Post-Adobe is fair; first/substantive needs verification.
"The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code" overstates "working front-end code" into production code before any customer has shipped it.
"Design-to-code has been promised for a decade and has repeatedly produced unmaintainable output" may be useful context, but it is not supplied here and needs sourcing.
"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" is too indirect for a live launch. The practical next move is fit-checking reporters once the proof gaps are answered.
gaps_in_B: "first big swing since the Adobe deal died" and "first major move" are invented unless someone verifies Figma has not made other major moves since the deal collapsed.
"a bet on staying independent" turns "no IPO timing disclosed" into a strategy claim. That is a nice narrative until a reporter asks who said it.
"A customer-story angle — `no_journalist_shape` as supplied" throws away a real enterprise-procurement angle. The problem is missing proof, not missing beat shape.
"clarity on exactly who needs a Make seat" is necessary but thin. The pricing angle also needs attach-rate, budget-owner, and bundling answers or it is just a price tag with adjectives removed.
